questions.question: <div style=\"text-align:justify\">If in a series LCR AC circuit, the rms voltage across L, C and R are V<sub>1<\/sub>, V<sub>2<\/sub> and V<sub>3<\/sub> respectively, then the voltage of the source is always :<\/div>$\n$
questions.explanation:
**Explain Question: A series LCR circuit has voltages V$\u$2081 (across L), V$\u$2082 (across C), and V$\u$2083 (across R). We must compare the source rms voltage with these individual rms voltages.
$ $**Concept: This question is based on phasor addition of voltages in AC circuits: VL and VC are 90° out of phase with VR and are opposite to each other, so voltages cannot be added algebraically—only vectorially.
$ $**Solution:
$ In$ a series LCR circuit:
$ $• VR is in phase with current.
$ $• VL leads current by 90°.
$ $• VC lags current by 90°.
$ Net$ reactive voltage = |VL – VC|.
$ Source$ voltage:
$ V$ = √( VR² + (VL – VC)² ).
$ This$ is always less than VL + VC + VR because phasor addition < arithmetic addition.
$ Thus$, source voltage is NOT equal to V$\u$2081 + V$\u$2082 + V$\u$2083 and also never more than that sum**.
$ Final$ Answer: (D)

$ $
